content: Treatment for infections caused by Chlamydia trachomatis involves the use of azithromycin and ceftriaxone. For Trichomonas vaginalis and bacterial vaginosis, metronidazole is the recommended treatment. All symptomatic women presenting with vaginal discharge, itching, or similar symptoms are treated for Trichomonas vaginalis. In the base case scenario, no additional costs are assumed to arise directly from antimicrobial resistance infections. However, a scenario was explored where all antibiotic prescriptions incur a cost, referred to as an antimicrobial resistance tax. This tax accounts for the broader costs of antimicrobial resistance, including future treatment costs for resistant infections, increased morbidity and mortality, and the costs of developing new treatments. This tax was applied to all individuals treated, regardless of whether the treatment was appropriate or not. The certainty of evidence regarding the effects of management guided by test results is categorized as very low, low, moderate, or high. The anticipated desirable effects of a syndromic approach to management are assessed as trivial, small, moderate, or large, with variations depending on the context. Diagnostic test accuracy and treatment data were used to model the effects on important outcomes, including among women with varying prevalence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. The magnitude of effects for each syndromic approach was assessed. The undesirable effects of the syndromic approach were also evaluated, ranging from large to trivial, with variability depending on the context. The values placed on the main outcomes by individuals were assessed for uncertainty or variability, with categories ranging from important uncertainty to no important uncertainty. The Guideline Development Group identified critical outcomes, including treatment rates (true positives), overtreatment (false positives), undertreatment (false negatives), true negatives, treatment side effects, antimicrobial resistance, and the identification of other reproductive diseases. The group prioritized the incidence of pelvic inflammatory disease due to missed cases but also considered the impact of overtreatment, which can contribute to increased antimicrobial resistance. Reproductive health outcomes, maternal outcomes, and infant and child outcomes were deemed important. Other considerations included coverage, patient and provider acceptability, and partner notification and treatment. For low prevalence settings (5% prevalence of N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis), favorable approaches included treating all women who test positive using rapid point-of-care tests with lower sensitivity (80%) and specificity (90%), or treating based on point-of-care test results among women with positive risk assessments or confirmed vaginal discharge on genital examination. Further favorable options included treatment based on positive speculum examination among women with positive risk assessments or confirmed vaginal discharge, or treatment based on positive speculum examination for all women. The WHO algorithm using speculum examination was the cheapest but resulted in the highest number of missed cases, leading to more pelvic inflammatory disease and moderate overtreatment. The WHO algorithm based on risk had trivial pelvic inflammatory disease and missed cases but moderate to high overtreatment, resulting in higher costs. For higher prevalence settings (20% prevalence of N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis), favorable approaches included treatment based on positive speculum or microscopy among women with positive risk assessments or confirmed vaginal discharge, treatment based on positive speculum or microscopy for all women, and treatment based on positive risk assessments or confirmed vaginal discharge. Slightly costlier but favorable options included treatment based on confirmed vaginal discharge by genital examination. Approaches with slightly higher pelvic inflammatory disease but not costly included treating all women who test positive on low-sensitivity and specificity point-of-care tests or treating all women who test positive on speculum examination. Health equity considerations revealed disparities in care-seeking behavior and testing based on socioeconomic and demographic factors. For example, symptomatic African-American women were more likely to be tested for STIs than symptomatic white women. Poor women in Mumbai, India, disproportionately sought treatment for vaginal discharge, often associated with problematic spousal relationships, abuse, and stress. In remote areas of South Africa with limited healthcare access, there was a significant burden of untreated symptomatic and asymptomatic STIs, highlighting the importance of mobile STI services. Socioeconomic status was linked to STI prevalence. Higher rates of chlamydia were observed in public health sector patients compared to private sector patients in Brazil, among illiterate women compared to those with higher education, and in rural versus urban areas. In the United States, an inverse relationship was found between education and the prevalence of chlamydia and gonorrhea among young women. Black women with college education had higher predicted probabilities of chlamydia or gonorrhea than white women with less than a high school diploma. Non-Hispanic African-Americans had significantly higher rates of bacterial vaginosis, C. trachomatis, and T. vaginalis compared to white Americans. Working women and spouses of unskilled workers had higher infection risks than homemakers and spouses of semi-skilled or skilled workers. Female adolescents in juvenile detention facilities had high chlamydia test positivity rates. Barriers to seeking treatment included stigma, fear, lack of awareness, cost, geographical access, lack of privacy, and dissatisfaction with previous care. Many women relied on self-treatment or delayed seeking care, with some waiting several months. Studies reported that 39–45% of women delayed seeking care for more than seven days. Syndromic management programs in Kenya and Tanzania effectively reduced STI incidence, and integrated networks of trained providers in Peru demonstrated feasibility and acceptability. However, challenges such as high staff turnover and gaps in provider knowledge and practice were noted in various settings, including Pakistan and Ethiopia. In summary, the implementation of syndromic management approaches for vaginal discharge has shown varying levels of feasibility, acceptability, and effectiveness across different settings. The balance of benefits, harms, and costs must be carefully considered, particularly in the context of antimicrobial resistance and health equity.
